_about: Presentation notes for the R-0412 sample. The dashboard merges this file into the UI payload when scenario_id is 'r0412'. It only adds plain-English wording, the code excerpt and the patch shown in the story; the trace, graph, prediction, safety and verification data all come from data/fixtures/r0412_revenue_growth.json. Strings here are trusted HTML.

say.compare: The agent was asked for revenue growth. It said revenue fell 88%. The right answer is that it grew about 18%.
say.dev: Found it. The page said 12,400, but the agent wrote down 1,240, ten times too small. Every step before this was right.
say.impact: One small slip, three wrong steps. Everything after step 5 inherited the bad number.
say.code: It opens the code behind step 5. One line reads the comma in “12,400” as a decimal point, so 12,400 becomes 12.4, then 1,240.
say.verdict: The answer is correct now: revenue grew 18.1%, and the original failure no longer happens.

tech.compare: assert growth ∈ [−50%, +80%] → FAIL · mismatched fields: revenue, growth
tech.dev: first_deviation = event_005 · output ≠ f(input) · upstream events 1–4 consistent

find.compare: revenue and growth are both wrong
find.code: extractor.py:42 reads “,” as a decimal point

evidence: + the cell is “12,400”, where “,” separates thousands
− no contradicting evidence found yet

test.name: test_thousands_separator
test.before: Fails before the fix: expected 12400, got 1240.

journey.title: How “12,400” became 1,240
steps: float() reads it as a decimal

n1.what: The request the agent was given. It also defines what a correct answer looks like: growth of about +18%, and a sanity check that growth stays between −50% and +80%.

n2.what: The agent planned three moves: fetch ACME’s investor page, pull out the revenue figure, then calculate growth. That plan is sensible, so the problem is not here.

n3.what: The agent downloaded ACME’s investor-relations page. It loaded successfully (HTTP 200), so the data source was available.

n4.what: The page’s table lists FY25 revenue as 12,400 (₹ lakh). This value is correct: good data reached the agent.
evidence: The value matches the source page, so the data reaching the agent was correct.

n5.what: The agent read the revenue cell and turned it into a number. It should have produced 12,400, but produced 1,240, ten times too small. Everything before this step was right; everything after it inherited the error.
n5.fixed: The agent now reads the revenue cell as 12,400, matching the page exactly.

n6.what: This step saved the extracted revenue for later steps. It worked exactly as designed. It just saved the wrong number it was handed, so it is affected, not broken.

n7.what: Calculated growth from this year’s revenue and last year’s (10,500). The maths is correct, but with 1,240 as input it produced −88.2%.
n7.fixed: With the correct input (12,400) it now calculates +18.1%.

n8.what: The agent wrote the answer: “Revenue fell 88.2%.” The link to step 7 is inferred: the sentence quotes the same growth figure.

n9.what: An automatic check that growth falls in a believable range (−50% to +80%). −88.2% is outside it, which is how this run was flagged as failed.
n9.fixed: +18.1% is inside the range, so the check now passes.

n10.what: The line of code that converts the revenue cell. It treats the comma in “12,400” as a decimal point, giving 12.4, then multiplies by 100 for the lakh unit, giving 1,240.
n10.fixed: The line now removes thousands separators before converting, so “12,400” becomes 12,400.

result_rows: “Extraction error” was ranked first and matched the cause.
extractor.py:42 read the thousands separator as a decimal point. Replay now matches the expected answer.
Other formats, like ₹ vs $ or lakh vs million.
Saved as INC-0412, provisional, and kept out of training until reviewed.
summary: R-0412: first deviation at step 5 (Extract value). Cause: extractor.py:42 treats the thousands separator in "12,400" as a decimal point (12.4 × 100 = 1240). Impact: 3 later steps. Fix: strip separators before int(). Verified on sample fixture v1 (simulated).
